# Three Sisters Planting

🌰 *Seedling. Captured fast after a conversation at the seed swap — may be half-remembered,
revisit before I plant in spring.*

The "Three Sisters" is a companion-planting technique from several Indigenous North American
agricultural traditions: **corn, beans, and squash** grown together in the same mound, each
doing a job the others can't.

- **Corn** grows tall and gives the beans a pole to climb. (Infrastructure.)
- **Beans** fix nitrogen from the air into the soil, feeding the heavy-feeding corn.
  (They pay rent.)
- **Squash** sprawls low with big leaves, shading out weeds and keeping moisture in.
  (Ground cover / DOS protection.)

## Why this is in *this* garden

Because it's a system where **cooperation removes the need for an external coordinator** —
no trellis to build, no fertilizer to truck in, less weeding. That's the exact lesson from
[[Compost Is a Distributed System]]: the most robust design is the one that needs the least
central management. Three plants, no manager, more food than any of them alone.

## To verify before I trust this note

- [ ] Actual spacing / mound size (I think ~12 in. between corn seeds?)
- [ ] Timing — corn first, then beans once corn is ~6 in.? Confirm.
- [ ] Which bean varieties climb vs. bush (bush beans won't use the corn).

When I've actually grown it once, this graduates to 🌿 budding.
